![](https://jadco.gov.jm/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/Group-3692x.webp)

## ANTI-DOPING RULE VIOLATIONS AND SANCTIONS

The World Anti-Doping Code defines doping as the occurrence of one or more of the Anti-Doping Rule Violations outlined in the Code. ‘Doping’ is more than simply using a prohibited substance or prohibited method. Currently, there are eleven (11) Anti-Doping Rule Violations.

**Anti-Doping Rule Violations**  
Athletes (and other individuals) are responsible for knowing what constitutes an Anti-Doping Rule Violation and the substances and methods which have been included on WADA’s Prohibited List.

**The following constitutes an Anti-Doping Rule Violation:**

* Presence of a prohibited substance (or its metabolites or markers) in an athlete’s sample.
* Use or attempted use by an athlete of a prohibited substance or prohibited method.
* Evading, refusing or failing to submit to sample collection.
* Whereabouts failures (Any combination of three ‘Filing Failures’ and/or ‘Missed Tests’ in a 12-month period).
* Tampering or attempted tampering with any part of doping control.
* Possession of prohibited substance or prohibited method.
* Trafficking or attempted trafficking in any prohibited substance or prohibited method.
* Administration or attempted administration to an athlete of any prohibited substance or prohibited method.
* Complicity or attempted complicity.
* Prohibited Association.
* Acts by an athlete or other person to discourage or retaliate against reporting to authorities.

## ANTI-DOPING SANCTIONS

A sanction is imposed by the Independent Anti-Doping Disciplinary Panel once an Anti-Doping Rule Violation has been determined.

**Length of Sanctions**  
Sanctions for Anti-Doping Rule Violations may range from a public reprimand to a lifetime ban. The period of ineligibility may vary depending on but not limited to the following:

**Anti-Doping Rule Violation.**

* The circumstance of an individual case, that is, the person’s degree of fault or negligence, and/or the seriousness of the violation.
* The substance and whether or not it is the first time the offence is being committed.
* Aggravating Circumstances.
* Results Management Agreements.
* Multiple Violations.

**The range of sanctions as stipulated by the World Anti-Doping Code includes:**

* Presence of prohibited substance/banned substance, its metabolites or markers in a sample: a reprimand and no period of ineligibility to maximum 4 years ineligibility from sport
* Possession of banned substances or method: a reprimand and no period of ineligibility to a maximum of 4 years ineligibility from sport
* Use or attempted use of prohibited substances or methods: a reprimand and no period of ineligibility to a maximum of 4 years ineligibility from sport
* Whereabouts: 1 to 2 years ineligibility from sport
* Evading, refusing or failing to submit to sample collection: a reprimand and no period of ineligibility to 4 years ineligibility from sport
* Tampering or attempted tampering with the doping control process: a reprimand and no period of ineligibility to 4 years ineligibility from sport
* Trafficking or attempted trafficking: a minimum of 4 years ineligibility from sport up to a lifetime ban
* Administration or attempted administration: a minimum of 4 years ineligibility from sport up to a lifetime ban
* Complicity or Attempted Complicity (assisting, encouraging, aiding, abetting, conspiring, covering up an Anti-Doping Rule Violation): a minimum of 2 years up to lifetime ineligibility
* Prohibited Association: 1 to 2 years ineligibility from sport
* Acts by an athlete or other person to discourage or retaliate against reporting to authorities: a minimum of 2 years to lifetime ineligibility

## CONSEQUENCES

The most common penalty for an Anti-Doping Rule Violation is a sanction imposing a period of ineligibility to participate in sport.

In addition to a period of ineligibility, there may be other consequences of committing an Anti-Doping Rule Violation. Such as:

* Automatic disqualification of individual results, including forfeiture of medals, points and prizes
* Disqualification of results in the event during which a violation occurs
* Disqualification of results in competitions subsequent to the initial test sample
* Ineligibility to compete in the next Olympic or Paralympic Games

**Consequences for Team Sport**  
If more than two members of a team in a Team Sport are found to have committed an Anti-Doping Rule Violation during an event period, the ruling body of the event shall impose an appropriate sanction on the team (e.g., loss of points, disqualification from a competition or event, or other sanction) in addition to any consequences imposed upon the individual athletes committing the Anti-Doping Rule Violation.

--- SOURCE 1: Sports Enhancement - The Hastings Center for Bioethics ---
URL: https://www.thehastingscenter.org/briefingbook/sports-enhancement

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from The Hastings Center for Bioethics is a comprehensive briefing on sports enhancement by Thomas H. Murray, PhD (President Emeritus of The Hastings Center). It examines the ethical dimensions of performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) in sport, going beyond simple condemnation to explore the complex moral landscape.

**Key Highlights:**
- The 2012 USADA "Reasoned Decision" exposed Lance Armstrong's systematic doping in professional cycling.
- Russia's organized doping and coverup at the 2014 Sochi Winter Olympics was documented, leading to sanctions against many Russian athletes.
- Public reaction to doping is split: some categorically condemn it as cheating, while others see entertainment value (e.g., more home runs).

**Arguments for Prohibiting PEDs:**
1. **The Significance of Rules in Sport:** Rules define which characteristics determine winners and losers. Equipment innovations (like fiberglass poles vs. banned super-slippery swimsuits) are evaluated based on continuity of skill requirements and equal opportunity.
2. **Natural Talents and Their Perfection:** The point of sport is to see how natural talents can be developed through intensive training, dedication, and smart tactics—not pharmacological shortcuts.
3. **The "Arms Race" in Sport:** PEDs create pressure on all athletes to use them, similar to an arms race, potentially leading to a public health catastrophe from high-dose, bizarre drug combinations.

**Emerging Challenges:**
- Clandestine drug developers creating undetectable substances (e.g., THG/"the clear" from the Balco lab).
- Hypoxic chambers that simulate high-altitude training.
- The prospect of gene doping using gene therapy techniques.
- High rates of adolescent non-therapeutic drug use (especially for cosmetic effects like looking "buff").

**Policy Recommendations:**
- More research on the culture of doping—why athletes, including youth, turn to drugs.
- Development of alternative strategies to encourage clean sport (e.g., biological passport systems).
- A revolution in sport governance demanding honesty and accountability from all actors, given the links between ethics, economics, and politics in elite sport.
</summary>

The article notes that the US cycling team (nine gold medals in 1984) and seven-time Tour de France winner (1999-2000) confessed to blood doping.

**Conclusion:** While rHu EPO improves oxygen-carrying capacity and aerobic performance, similar benefits are achievable through endurance training. The health risks are severe, including mortality. The authors call for more research on the harmful effects of EPO abuse and emphasize that athletes, coaches, and team doctors should discourage such artificial methods of performance enhancement.

Key figures like Sports Minister Manfred Ewald and top sports doctor Manfred Höppner were convicted of causing bodily harm to athletes. Former athletes have since sought and received financial compensation from the German government, including a 13.65 million euro fund established in 2016. The IOC declined to revise Olympic medal records despite petitions from the US and Great Britain. --- SOURCE 21: Mechanics of Oscar Pistorius's running blades - Wikipedia ---
URL: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mechanics_of_Oscar_Pistorius%27s_running_blades

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Wikipedia article examines the mechanics of the carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer running blades (Flex-Foot Cheetah prosthetics) used by South African Paralympic runner Oscar Pistorius, who has double below-the-knee amputations and became the first amputee sprinter to compete in the Olympic Games (2012).

**Background:** Pistorius began running in 2004 after a rugby injury and was fitted with Össur carbon-fibre blades. The blades are transtibial prostheses that store kinetic energy like a spring. They are made from layers of carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer (30-90 sheets depending on athlete weight), autoclaved to fuse into a solid plate, and bolted to custom carbon-fibre sockets. Each limb costs $15-18,000 USD.

**How the blades work:** Unlike able-bodied sprinters who use calves and ankles to return energy from hips and knees, Pistorius must generate roughly twice the power from his gluteal and quadriceps muscles. About 85% of his power comes from his hips. The blades compress under his weight and release forward thrust as they return to shape. He is slow out of the blocks because the flexible blades don't provide horizontal thrust, requiring him to pop straight up. He compensates for the lack of ankles on turns by breaking curves into short straight lines.

**Advantage/Disadvantage Debate:** The IAAF initially banned the blades in 2008 after the Brüggemann study found Pistorius used ~25% less energy expenditure, that the blades returned nearly 3x more energy than a human ankle, and that energy loss in the blade was 9.3% vs. 42.4% in a normal ankle. However, the Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstated him after the Weyand et al. study (2008) found his energy usage was 3.8% lower than elite distance runners and 17% lower than non-disabled 400m sprinters, concluding that running on blades is "physiologically similar but mechanically different" from biological legs. The Weyand study also found Pistorius re-positioned his legs 15.7% faster than most world record sprinters. A follow-up Grabowski study (2009) found that single running blades reduced ground force production by 9%, limiting top speed.

**2012 Paralympics Controversy:** Brazilian runner Alan Oliveira and USA runner Blake Leeper switched to longer running blades before the 2012 Paralympics, leading to marked improvement. Pistorius complained that longer blades provided artificially lengthened strides. Oliveira's stride length was 2.2m vs. Pistorius's 2.0m (9% longer), though Oliveira took more strides (99 vs. 92).

**Research limitations:** Studies were conducted on level treadmills and did not measure performance from starting blocks, on curved tracks, or account for physiological differences between amputees and non-amputees.
</summary>

This Britannica article explores the history and debate around performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) and technological augmentation in sports. It traces PED use back to ancient Olympic athletes who consumed animal hearts, hallucinogenic mushrooms, and other substances. **Con Arguments:**
1. PEDs and smart technology violate the spirit and integrity of sport, shifting competition from skill to "how good your doctor is."
2. PEDs are dangerous, causing heart damage, stroke, psychosis, and death (e.g., bodybuilding deaths far exceed MMA fatalities).

URL: https://www.mayoclinic.org/healthy-lifestyle/fitness/in-depth/performance-enhancing-drugs/art-20046134

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Mayo Clinic article provides a comprehensive overview of the risks associated with performance-enhancing drugs (doping) in sports. It covers eight categories of substances:

**Anabolic Steroids:** Synthetic forms of testosterone used to boost strength and muscle mass. Risks include infertility, breast development in men, testicular shrinkage, increased body hair in women, stunted growth in teens, heart problems, and legal consequences.

**Androstenedione (Andro):** A hormone that converts to testosterone. Studies show it doesn't boost strength. Side effects include heart damage, increased risk of heart attack and stroke, acne, and hormonal imbalances.

**Human Growth Hormone (HGH/Somatotropin):** Used to build muscle but lacks proof of effectiveness for athletic performance. Side effects include nerve pain, high cholesterol, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, and increased cancer risk.

**Erythropoietin (EPO/Epoetin):** Increases red blood cell count and oxygen delivery to muscles. Linked to at least 18 deaths among pro cyclists in the 1990s. Risks include stroke, heart attack, and pulmonary artery blockages.

**Diuretics:** Used to lose water weight and mask other drugs in urine tests. Side effects include dizziness, dehydration, headaches, nausea, and can be fatal when used for doping.

**Creatine:** A supplement that may help with short-term power bursts (e.g., weightlifting, sprinting). Generally safe for healthy adults at recommended doses, but can cause weight gain, cramps, and dehydration.

**Stimulants:** Include caffeine, amphetamines, and drugs like cocaine. Boost brain chemicals and heart rate. Side effects include tremors, insomnia, anxiety, addiction, weight loss, heart damage, and stroke.

The article concludes that the long-term effects of performance-enhancing drugs haven't been adequately studied, and any short-term benefits come with serious health risks. Doping is banned by most sports organizations and is illegal.
</summary>

This opinion piece argues against legalizing performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) in sport, specifically cycling, while engaging with the pro-legalization arguments of Oxford ethics professor Julian Savulescu. The author presents several key arguments against legalization:

1. **Health Risks**: Most banned substances are banned for legitimate health reasons. Growth hormone, for example, raises cancer and heart disease risk at performance-enhancing doses.

2. **Competitive Dynamics**: Unlike alcohol prohibition, doping is about gaining an edge. If one athlete uses a "tipple" of EPO, others will binge-inject megadoses to compete.

3. **Practical Barriers**: Many PEDs like EPO are regulated pharmaceuticals unavailable without medical prescription. A doctor cannot prescribe them for sports use.

The author argues this approach was tried in cycling during the 1990s with a 50% haematocrit limit and failed — riders gamed the system by diluting their blood to pass tests while riding with dangerously high levels. The 50% limit became a competitive minimum rather than an upper ceiling.

The author concludes that the current anti-doping regime, while imperfect, acts as a "net" that filters out some of the worst excesses and protects both health and the business of sport. # Summary: Recreational and Performance Enhancing Drugs in Sport

This Physiopedia article covers two main categories of drug use in sports: recreational drug use and performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs).

## Recreational Drug Use in Sports
Illicit recreational drug use is a significant issue in Western society. In Australia, 38% of people report using an illicit drug at least once in their lifetime, with higher rates in the 20–29 age group. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) provides an updated list of prohibited substances, including alcohol, beta-blockers, anabolic agents, peptide hormones, stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids, and others. The most commonly used recreational drugs in sports are alcohol, cigarettes, and cannabis (particularly among adolescents).

**Prevalence/Incidence:** Use varies across levels and types of sports. Athletes use these substances to enhance cognition, stamina, strength, and power. Sports participation is more associated with alcohol use but negatively associated with cigarette or illicit drug use. High-contact sports correlate with increased risk for substance abuse.

**Prevention measures** include after-school community activities, increasing parental involvement, educating parents and children about communication, and strengthening support networks.

## Performance Enhancing Drugs (PEDs)
Regulatory bodies report 5% to 31% of athletes use PEDs. Current data suggests 14-39% of athletes utilize PEDs. Commonly abused agents include anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS), blood, erythropoietin, growth hormone, nutritional supplements, creatine, amphetamines, stimulants, and analgesics. PEDs and dietary supplements are not regulated by the USFDA.

**Adverse effects** of PEDs include violent behavior, suicide attempts, hypertension, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures, and death. AAS side effects in men include acne, testicular atrophy, infertility, gynecomastia, and liver toxicity. In women: facial hair growth, voice deepening, menstrual irregularities, and genital enlargement. Psychosocial effects include depression, mania, aggression, psychotic episodes, and dependence syndrome.

**Epidemiology:** AAS use is significantly more common in males, while dietary supplement use is higher in females. The highest rates of PED use in the US are in the South Atlantic region. AAS use is negatively correlated with age, education level, and number of children. Adolescents abusing AAS may progress to opioid use later in life.

**Testing:** AAS detection uses urine immunoassay measuring testosterone:epitestosterone ratio (must be <2:1, upper limit 6:1). Human growth hormone and EPO are difficult to detect.

**Treatment:** Involves periodic weaning of the substance to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Long-term AAS abusers may need artificial testosterone supplementation.

**Clinical Bottom Line:** PEDs are used by athletes of all levels. Healthcare professionals, coaches, and athletes share responsibility for education and prevention of PEDs abuse.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This narrative review examines psychotropic substance use among elite athletes, focusing on prevalence, patterns, causes, and risk factors. The review found that the most commonly used psychoactive substances among elite athletes are alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, stimulants, and prescription opioids. Overall consumption rates are lower in professional sports than the general population, but specific substances like smokeless tobacco, prescription opioids, and stimulants show high prevalence in certain sports.

Key findings by substance:
- **Nicotine**: Combustible tobacco use is lower among athletes, but smokeless tobacco (snus, chewing tobacco) is highly prevalent in winter sports and US baseball (over a third of MLB players). Active nicotine use was found in 15% of athletes across sports, with up to 55% in strength-based and winter sports.
- **Cannabis**: WADA testing shows low rates, but self-report surveys suggest higher consumption. Use is more common in winter and team sports, with low rates in endurance sports.
- **Opioids**: Recreational opioid abuse appears uncommon, but prescription opioid misuse is elevated among US college athletes and former NFL players (over half reported use during career, 70% of those misused). Low-potency opioids like tramadol are not banned by WADA.
- **Alcohol**: Most frequently consumed substance. College athletes show higher consumption and binge drinking rates than non-athletes. Use is higher in team sports and outside competition season.
- **Stimulants**: Therapeutic use exemptions for ADHD stimulants have increased significantly. Illicit stimulants like cocaine are rare according to doping tests but anecdotal evidence suggests otherwise.

Data sources include WADA drug testing (only 0.25% of 322,050 tests in 2017 positive for stimulants, narcotics, or cannabinoids) and self-report surveys, which show much higher rates. The review notes significant knowledge gaps, particularly regarding prevalence of substance use disorders, and calls for specific preventive and therapeutic concepts for elite athletes. The authors emphasize the need for large-sample longitudinal studies combining self-report and urine testing, and for sports medicine to integrate mental health treatment.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Mayo Clinic article provides a comprehensive overview of the risks associated with performance-enhancing drugs (doping) in sports. It covers eight categories of substances:

**Anabolic Steroids:** Synthetic forms of testosterone used to boost strength and muscle mass. Risks include infertility, breast development in men, testicular shrinkage, increased body hair in women, stunted growth in teens, heart problems, and legal consequences.

**Androstenedione (Andro):** A hormone that converts to testosterone. Studies show it doesn't boost strength. Side effects include heart damage, increased risk of heart attack and stroke, acne, and hormonal imbalances.

**Human Growth Hormone (HGH/Somatotropin):** Used to build muscle but lacks proof of effectiveness for athletic performance. Side effects include nerve pain, high cholesterol, joint pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, and increased cancer risk.

**Erythropoietin (EPO/Epoetin):** Increases red blood cell count and oxygen delivery to muscles. Linked to at least 18 deaths among pro cyclists in the 1990s. Risks include stroke, heart attack, and pulmonary artery blockages.

**Diuretics:** Used to lose water weight and mask other drugs in urine tests. Side effects include dizziness, dehydration, headaches, nausea, and can be fatal when used for doping.

**Creatine:** A supplement that may help with short-term power bursts (e.g., weightlifting, sprinting). Generally safe for healthy adults at recommended doses, but can cause weight gain, cramps, and dehydration.

**Stimulants:** Include caffeine, amphetamines, and drugs like cocaine. Boost brain chemicals and heart rate. Side effects include tremors, insomnia, anxiety, addiction, weight loss, heart damage, and stroke.

The article concludes that the long-term effects of performance-enhancing drugs haven't been adequately studied, and any short-term benefits come with serious health risks. Doping is banned by most sports organizations and is illegal.
</summary>

# Summary: Recreational and Performance Enhancing Drugs in Sport

This Physiopedia article covers two main categories of drug use in sports: recreational drug use and performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs).

## Recreational Drug Use in Sports
Illicit recreational drug use is a significant issue in Western society. In Australia, 38% of people report using an illicit drug at least once in their lifetime, with higher rates in the 20–29 age group. The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) provides an updated list of prohibited substances, including alcohol, beta-blockers, anabolic agents, peptide hormones, stimulants, narcotics, cannabinoids, and others. The most commonly used recreational drugs in sports are alcohol, cigarettes, and cannabis (particularly among adolescents).

**Prevalence/Incidence:** Use varies across levels and types of sports. Athletes use these substances to enhance cognition, stamina, strength, and power. Sports participation is more associated with alcohol use but negatively associated with cigarette or illicit drug use. High-contact sports correlate with increased risk for substance abuse.

**Prevention measures** include after-school community activities, increasing parental involvement, educating parents and children about communication, and strengthening support networks.

## Performance Enhancing Drugs (PEDs)
Regulatory bodies report 5% to 31% of athletes use PEDs. Current data suggests 14-39% of athletes utilize PEDs. Commonly abused agents include anabolic-androgenic steroids (AAS), blood, erythropoietin, growth hormone, nutritional supplements, creatine, amphetamines, stimulants, and analgesics. PEDs and dietary supplements are not regulated by the USFDA.

**Adverse effects** of PEDs include violent behavior, suicide attempts, hypertension, arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, stroke, seizures, and death. AAS side effects in men include acne, testicular atrophy, infertility, gynecomastia, and liver toxicity. In women: facial hair growth, voice deepening, menstrual irregularities, and genital enlargement. Psychosocial effects include depression, mania, aggression, psychotic episodes, and dependence syndrome.

**Epidemiology:** AAS use is significantly more common in males, while dietary supplement use is higher in females. The highest rates of PED use in the US are in the South Atlantic region. AAS use is negatively correlated with age, education level, and number of children. Adolescents abusing AAS may progress to opioid use later in life.

**Testing:** AAS detection uses urine immunoassay measuring testosterone:epitestosterone ratio (must be <2:1, upper limit 6:1). Human growth hormone and EPO are difficult to detect.

**Treatment:** Involves periodic weaning of the substance to avoid withdrawal symptoms. Long-term AAS abusers may need artificial testosterone supplementation.

**Clinical Bottom Line:** PEDs are used by athletes of all levels. Healthcare professionals, coaches, and athletes share responsibility for education and prevention of PEDs abuse.
</summary>

This narrative review examines psychotropic substance use among elite athletes, focusing on prevalence, patterns, causes, and risk factors. Overall consumption rates are lower in professional sports than the general population, but specific substances like smokeless tobacco, prescription opioids, and stimulants show high prevalence in certain sports.

- **Nicotine**: Combustible tobacco use is lower among athletes, but smokeless tobacco (snus, chewing tobacco) is highly prevalent in winter sports and US baseball (over a third of MLB players). Data sources include WADA drug testing (only 0.25% of 322,050 tests in 2017 positive for stimulants, narcotics, or cannabinoids) and self-report surveys, which show much higher rates. **Benjamin Sinclair Johnson**, [CM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Canada "Order of Canada") [OOnt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Ontario "Order of Ontario") (born December 30, 1961) is a Canadian former [sprinter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sprint_(running) "Sprint (running)"). During the 1987–88 season he held the title of the world's fastest man, breaking both the 100 m and the 60 m indoor World Records. He won the 100 metres at the 1987 World Championships in Athletics, and again at the 1988 Summer Olympics, but was disqualified for doping and stripped of the gold medals. He was the first to beat the 9.9 and 9.8 seconds barrier.

He won two bronze medals at the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics"), as well as gold medals at the [1985 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1985_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "1985 IAAF World Indoor Championships"), [1986 Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Goodwill_Games "1986 Goodwill Games") and [1986 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1986_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 1986 Commonwealth Games"). He was trained by [Charlie Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Francis "Charlie Francis").

Benjamin Johnson was born in [Falmouth, Jamaica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Falmouth,_Jamaica "Falmouth, Jamaica"), and emigrated to Canada in 1976.[[2]](#cite_note-2) He grew up in the [Lawrence Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Heights "Lawrence Heights") community of [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"),[[3]](#cite_note-3) before later residing in the suburb of [Scarborough, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scarborough,_Ontario "Scarborough, Ontario"). His early life was met with challenges regarding his Black immigrant status in a white-dominant society, which built up to lead him to beg his parents to emigrate back; however, he decided to stay.[[4]](#cite_note-Early_Life-4)

Johnson met coach [Charlie Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Francis "Charlie Francis") and joined the Scarborough Optimists track and field club, training at [York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_University "York University"). Francis was a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") 100 metres sprint champion himself (1970, 1971 and 1973) and a member of the Canadian team for the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"). Francis was also Canada's national sprint coach for nine years.

Johnson's first international success came when he won 2 [silver medals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal") at the [1982 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1982_Commonwealth_Games "1982 Commonwealth Games") in [Brisbane, Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brisbane,_Australia "Brisbane, Australia"). He finished behind [Allan Wells](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allan_Wells "Allan Wells") of Scotland in the 100 metres with a time of 10.05 seconds and was a member of the Canadian 4 × 100 metres relay team which finished behind Nigeria. This success was not repeated at the [1983 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1983 World Championships in Athletics") in [Helsinki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helsinki "Helsinki"), where he was eliminated in the semi-finals, finishing 6th with a time of 10.44, nor at the [1983 Pan American Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983_Pan_American_Games "1983 Pan American Games") in [Caracas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caracas "Caracas") where Johnson placed 5th in the 100 metres final with a time of 10.25.

At the [1984 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Summer_Olympics "1984 Summer Olympics") in Los Angeles, he reached the 100 metres final; after a false start, he won the bronze medal behind [Carl Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Lewis "Carl Lewis") and [Sam Graddy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Graddy "Sam Graddy") with a time of 10.22. He also won a bronze medal with the Canadian [4 × 100 m relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_×_100_metres_relay "4 × 100 metres relay") team of Johnson, [Tony Sharpe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tony_Sharpe "Tony Sharpe"), [Desai Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Desai_Williams "Desai Williams") and [Sterling Hinds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sterling_Hinds "Sterling Hinds"), who ran a time of 38.70. By the end of the 1984 season, Johnson had established himself as Canada's top sprinter, and on August 22 in [Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zürich "Zürich"), [Switzerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Switzerland "Switzerland"), he bettered Williams' Canadian record of 10.17 by running 10.12.

In 1985, after eight consecutive losses, Johnson finally beat Carl Lewis. Other success against Lewis included the 1986 [Goodwill Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goodwill_Games "Goodwill Games"), where Johnson beat Lewis, running 9.95 for first place, against Lewis' third-place time of 10.06. He broke [Houston McTear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Houston_McTear "Houston McTear")'s seven-year-old world record in the [60 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/60_metres "60 metres") in 1986, with a time of 6.50 seconds.[[5]](#cite_note-5) He also won Commonwealth gold at the 1986 games in [Edinburgh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edinburgh "Edinburgh"), beating [Linford Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linford_Christie "Linford Christie") for the 100 metres title with a time of 10.07. Johnson also led the Canadian 4 × 100 metres relay team to gold, and won a bronze in the 200 metres. Also in 1986, Canadian sprinter [Mike Dwyer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Dwyer_(athlete) "Mike Dwyer (athlete)") expressed concern that the use of drugs had reached "epidemic proportions" among Canadian sprinters, particularly among those who trained in the Toronto area. [Atlee Mahorn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlee_Mahorn "Atlee Mahorn") also speculated that many sprinters were on steroids.[[6]](#cite_note-6)

On April 29, 1987, Johnson was invested as a Member of the [Order of Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Canada "Order of Canada"). "World record holder for the indoor 60-metre run, this Ontarian has proved himself to be the world's fastest human being and has broken Canadian, Commonwealth and World Cup 100-metre records," it read. "Recipient of the Norton Crowe Award for Male Athlete of the Year for 1985, 'Big Ben' was the winner of the 1986 Lou Marsh Trophy as Canada's top athlete."

By the time of the [1987 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1987 World Championships in Athletics"), Johnson had won his four previous races with Lewis and had established himself as the best 100 metres sprinter. At Rome, Johnson gained instant world fame and confirmed this status when he beat Lewis for the title, setting a new world record of 9.83 seconds as well, beating [Calvin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Smith "Calvin Smith")'s [former record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Record_progression_100_m_men "World Record progression 100 m men") by a full tenth of a second.

After Rome, Johnson became a lucrative marketing celebrity. According to coach Charlie Francis, after breaking the world record, Johnson earned about $480,000 a month in endorsements.[[7]](#cite_note-7) Johnson won both the [Lou Marsh Trophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lou_Marsh_Trophy "Lou Marsh Trophy") and [Lionel Conacher Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lionel_Conacher_Award "Lionel Conacher Award"), and was named the [Associated Press Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Associated_Press_Athlete_of_the_Year "Associated Press Athlete of the Year") for 1987.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Following Johnson's defeat of Lewis in Rome, Lewis started trying to explain away his defeat. He first claimed that Johnson had false-started, then he alluded to a stomach virus which had weakened him. Finally, without naming names, Lewis said "There are a lot of people coming out of nowhere. I don't think they are doing it without drugs." This was the start of Lewis' calling on the sport of track and field to be cleaned up in terms of the illegal use of performance-enhancing drugs. While cynics noted that the problem had been in the sport for many years, they pointed out that it did not become a cause for Lewis until he was actually defeated, with some also pointing to Lewis's egotistical attitude and lack of humility. During a controversial interview with the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC"), Lewis said:[[9]](#cite_note-times-9)

> There are gold medallists at this meet who are on drugs, that [100 metres] race will be looked at for many years, for more reasons than one.

Johnson's response was:

> When Carl Lewis was winning everything, I never said a word against him. And when the next guy comes along and beats me, I won't complain about that either.

This set up the rivalry leading into the 1988 Olympic Games.

In 1988, Johnson experienced a number of setbacks to his running career. In February of that year he pulled a hamstring, and in May he aggravated the same injury. Meanwhile, in Paris in June, Lewis ran a 9.99. Then in Zurich, Switzerland on August 17, the two faced each other for the first time since the [1987 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1987 World Championships in Athletics"); Lewis won in 9.93, while Johnson finished third in 10.00. "The gold medal for the (Olympic) 100 metres is mine," Carl Lewis said. "I will never again lose to Johnson."[[9]](#cite_note-times-9)

### Olympic Games and subsequent disqualification

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Olympic Games and subsequent disqualification")]

On September 24, 1988, Johnson won the [100 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1988_Summer_Olympics_–_Men's_100_metres "Athletics at the 1988 Summer Olympics – Men's 100 metres") at the [Summer Olympics in Seoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Summer_Olympics "1988 Summer Olympics"), lowering his own world record to 9.79 seconds. He was the first Canadian sprinter since [Percy Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Williams_(sprinter) "Percy Williams (sprinter)") in 1928 to win the 100 metres at the Olympics. Johnson later remarked that he would have been even faster if he hadn't raised his hand in the air just before he hit the tape.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

However, [Park Jong-sei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_Jong-sei "Park Jong-sei") of the Olympic Doping Control Center found that Johnson's urine sample contained [stanozolol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanozolol "Stanozolol"), and he was disqualified three days after the race.[[11]](#cite_note-11) He later admitted having used steroids when he ran his 1987 world record, which caused the [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF "IAAF") to rescind that record as well. Johnson and coach Francis complained that they used performance-enhancing agents in order to remain on equal footing with the other top athletes. In testimony before the [Dubin inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubin_inquiry "Dubin inquiry") into drug use in sport, Francis charged that Johnson was only one of many cheaters, and he just happened to get caught. Often dubbed "the dirtiest race in history," the 1988 100 m final had only two out of a total of eight runners who remained clean throughout their careers (Calvin Smith and Robson da Silva).[[12]](#cite_note-12)[[13]](#cite_note-13)[[14]](#cite_note-14)

Johnson's coach, [Charlie Francis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Francis "Charlie Francis"), a vocal critic of the IOC testing procedures, is the author of *Speed Trap*, which features Johnson heavily. In the book, he freely admits that his athletes were taking [anabolic steroids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anabolic_steroids "Anabolic steroids"), as he claims all top athletes at the time were, and also claims that Johnson could not possibly have tested positive for that particular steroid since Johnson actually preferred [furazabol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Furazabol "Furazabol"). He thought stanozolol made his body "feel tight".[[15]](#cite_note-15) The numerous athletes using performance-enhancing drugs at the time understood how long before a race, and possible drug test, they should stop using the drugs. Johnson later claimed that André A. Jackson, Lewis' [Santa Monica Track Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Track_Club "Santa Monica Track Club") teammate, who was inside the drug testing room in Seoul, may have placed the stanozolol in one of the beers Johnson drank in order to make urine for his test. He admitted he gave him beer. His response to the stanozolol blame: "Of course I can say I didn't. But I can also say I did, too. What's the benefit?"[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17)

During an interview on the Toronto Mike'd Podcast, Johnson said the fact he switched sponsorships from [Adidas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adidas "Adidas") to [Diadora](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diadora "Diadora") may have been a factor in having his medal stripped. Johnson suggested Adidas athletes were more protected versus athletes aligned with smaller companies like Diadora.[[18]](#cite_note-18)

On 28 September 2018, the Toronto Star ran an article on the lab report which was created on Johnson's sample during the 1988 Olympic Games. It was produced by the IOC Doping Control Center in Seoul two days after Johnson handed in a urine sample taken after the 100 m final. The newspaper concluded that the assumed substance Stanozolol was traceable, but "inconsistencies" are found in the report. The Toronto Star article goes on to state that no Canadian Olympic team official saw the lab report in Seoul. The lab report was requested by Canada's chief medical officer, Dr. William Stanish. The Canadian team did not object after the IOC Medical Commission assured "that its testing methods were unassailable."[[19]](#cite_note-19)

#### Canadian reaction

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Canadian reaction")]

Canadians initially rejoiced in the reflected glory of winning the gold medal and breaking the world record.[[20]](#cite_note-20) Canadian Prime Minister [Brian Mulroney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Mulroney "Brian Mulroney") watched Johnson set the new world record and after the race congratulated him over the phone. "It's a marvellous evening for Canada," Mulroney said in the televised conversation.[[21]](#cite_note-21) Newspapers covered the occasion by concocting words such as "Benfastic" (*Toronto Star*, September 25, 1988) to describe it.

Two days later, Canadians witnessed the downfall of Johnson, when he was stripped of his gold medal and world record. [Mark Tewksbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Tewksbury "Mark Tewksbury"), a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") Olympic swimmer hung a bed sheet banner out of his Olympic Village apartment window expressing 'Hero to Zero in 9.79'. In the first week following the disqualification, Canadian newspapers devoted several pages a day to the story. One headline right after the exposure asked "Why, Ben?" (*Toronto Sun*, September 26, 1988). Because of the Olympic scandal, the Canadian news agency *[Canadian Press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Press "Canadian Press")* named Johnson "[Newsmaker of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Newsmaker_of_the_Year "Canadian Newsmaker of the Year")" for 1988.

### Competitors implicated in doping controversies

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Competitors implicated in doping controversies")]

Johnson was not the only participant whose success was questioned: [Carl Lewis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Lewis "Carl Lewis") had tested positive at the [Olympic Trials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_Trials_(track_and_field) "United States Olympic Trials (track and field)") for [pseudoephedrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pseudoephedrine "Pseudoephedrine"), [ephedrine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephedrine "Ephedrine") and [phenylpropanolamine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenylpropanolamine "Phenylpropanolamine"). Lewis defended himself, claiming that he had accidentally consumed the banned substances. After the supplements that he had taken were analyzed to prove his claims, the USOC accepted his claim of inadvertent use, since a dietary supplement he ingested was found to contain "Ma huang", the Chinese name for [Ephedra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ephedra_(medicine) "Ephedra (medicine)") (ephedrine is known to help weight loss).[[22]](#cite_note-:0-22) Fellow [Santa Monica Track Club](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica_Track_Club "Santa Monica Track Club") teammates [Joe DeLoach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_DeLoach "Joe DeLoach") and [Floyd Heard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floyd_Heard "Floyd Heard") were also found to have the same banned stimulants in their systems, and were cleared to compete for the same reason.[[23]](#cite_note-23)[[24]](#cite_note-autogenerated1-24)

The highest level of the stimulants Lewis recorded was 6 ppm, which was regarded as a positive test in 1988 but is now regarded as negative test. The acceptable level has been raised to 10 parts per million for ephedrine and twenty-five parts per million for other substances.[[22]](#cite_note-:0-22) According to the IOC rules at the time, positive tests with levels lower than 10 ppm were cause of further investigation but not immediate ban. Neal Benowitz, a professor of medicine at UC San Francisco who is an expert on ephedrine and other stimulants, agreed that "These [levels] are what you'd see from someone taking cold or allergy medicines and are unlikely to have any effect on performance."[[22]](#cite_note-:0-22)

Following Exum's revelations the IAAF acknowledged that at the 1988 Olympic Trials the USOC indeed followed the correct procedures in dealing with eight positive findings for ephedrine and ephedrine-related compounds in low concentration.

[Linford Christie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linford_Christie "Linford Christie") was found to have [metabolites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metabolite "Metabolite") of pseudoephedrine in his urine after a 200 m heat at the same Olympics, but was later cleared of any wrongdoing.[[25]](#cite_note-25)[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27) Of the top five competitors in the race, only former world record holder and eventual bronze medalist [Calvin Smith](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calvin_Smith "Calvin Smith") never failed a drug test during his career. Smith later said: "I should have been the gold medalist."[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29)

#### The Dubin Inquiry

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: The Dubin Inquiry")]

After the Seoul test, Johnson initially denied doping, but, testifying before the 1989 [Dubin inquiry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubin_inquiry "Dubin inquiry"), a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") government investigation into drug abuse, he admitted that he had lied. Charlie Francis, his coach, told the inquiry that Johnson had been using steroids since 1981. Before that, his personal best (without drugs) was 10.25 which was good for a teenager back then, fast enough for third place in the Weltklasse Zürich meeting 1985 and 1986, for instance.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

In Canada, the federal government established the Commission of Inquiry Into the Use of Drugs and Banned Practices Intended to Increase Athletic Performance, headed by Ontario Appeal Court Chief Justice [Charles Dubin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dubin "Charles Dubin"). The Dubin Inquiry (as it became known), which was televised live, heard hundreds of hours of testimony about the widespread use of performance-enhancing drugs among athletes. The inquiry began in January 1989 and lasted 91 days, with 122 witnesses called, including athletes, coaches, sport administrators, IOC representatives, doctors and government officials.

### Comeback

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Comeback")]

In 1991, after his suspension ended, he attempted a comeback. He returned to the track for the Hamilton Indoor Games in 1991 and was greeted by the largest crowd to ever attend an indoor Canadian track and field event. More than 17,000 people saw him finish second in the 50 metres in 5.77 seconds.

He failed to qualify for the [1991 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1991_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1991 World Championships in Athletics") in Tokyo but made the Canadian Olympic team again in 1992 in Barcelona, Spain after finishing second at the Canadian Olympic trials to [Bruny Surin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruny_Surin "Bruny Surin").[[31]](#cite_note-31) He missed the 100 metre finals at the [Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics "1992 Summer Olympics"), however, finishing last in his semi-final heat after stumbling out of the blocks.

In 1993, he won the 50 metres on January 7 in Grenoble, France, in 5.65 seconds, just 0.04 seconds shy of the world record. However, he was again found guilty of doping just after the race – this time for excess testosterone – and was subsequently banned for life by the [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF "IAAF"). Federal amateur sport minister [Pierre Cadieux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Cadieux "Pierre Cadieux") called Johnson a national disgrace, and suggested he consider moving back to Jamaica. Johnson commented that it was "by far the most disgusting comment [he had] ever heard".[[32]](#cite_note-32) In April 1999, a [Canadian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadians "Canadians") adjudicator ruled that there were procedural errors in Johnson's lifetime ban and allowed him to appeal. The decision meant Johnson could technically run in Canada but nobody would compete against him. They would be considered "contaminated" by the IAAF and could also face sanctions. On June 12, 1999, Johnson entered a track meet in [Kitchener](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kitchener,_Ontario "Kitchener, Ontario"), Ontario, and was forced to run alone, against the clock. He posted a time of 11.0 seconds. In late 1999, Johnson failed a drug test for the third time by testing positive for [hydrochlorothiazide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrochlorothiazide "Hydrochlorothiazide"), a banned [diuretic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diuretic "Diuretic") that can be used to mask the presence of other drugs. Johnson had not competed since 1993 and had arranged the test himself as part of his efforts to be reinstated.

In 1999, Johnson made headlines again when it was revealed that he had been hired by [Libyan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libya "Libya") leader [Muammar Gaddafi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muammar_Gaddafi "Muammar Gaddafi") to act as a personal trainer for his son, [Al-Saadi Gaddafi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Saadi_Gaddafi "Al-Saadi Gaddafi"), who aspired to join [Perugia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AC_Perugia_Calcio "AC Perugia Calcio"), an Italian football club. Al-Saadi ultimately did join Perugia but was sacked after one game when he failed a drug test. Johnson's publicist in Canada had predicted in *[The Globe and Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Globe_and_Mail "The Globe and Mail")* that his training of the young Gaddafi would earn Johnson a [Nobel Peace Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Peace_Prize "Nobel Peace Prize").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

### Late 1990s and beyond

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Late 1990s and beyond")]

Johnson briefly acted as trainer for [Argentine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Argentina "Argentina") football player [Diego Maradona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diego_Maradona "Diego Maradona") in 1997. This occurred at [York University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/York_University "York University"), [Toronto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto").[[33]](#cite_note-33)

In 1998, Johnson appeared in a charity race in [Charlottetown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlottetown "Charlottetown"), [Prince Edward Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Edward_Island "Prince Edward Island"), where he raced against a thoroughbred race horse, a harness racing horse and a stock car.[[34]](#cite_note-34) Johnson finished third in the race.

According to a 1998 article in *[Outside](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Outside_(magazine) "Outside (magazine)")* magazine, Johnson spent much of the latter part of the 1990s living downstairs in the house he shared with his mother Gloria. He spent his leisure time reading, watching movies, and taking his mother to church. He lived in a spacious home in [Newmarket, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Newmarket,_Ontario "Newmarket, Ontario")'s Stonehaven neighborhood. He claims to have lost his [Ferrari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferrari "Ferrari") when he used it as collateral for a loan from an acquaintance in order to make a house payment.[[35]](#cite_note-35) His mother died of cancer in 2004 and Johnson lived with his sister afterwards.

Shortly after his leaving Libya, it was reported that Johnson had been robbed of $7,300 by a [Romani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romani_people "Romani people") gang in [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rome "Rome"). His wallet was taken, containing $7,300 in cash, the proceeds of his pay for training Gaddafi. Johnson gave chase, but was unable to catch them after they vanished into a metro station.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

In May 2005, Johnson launched a clothing and sports supplement line, the *Ben Johnson Collection*. The motto for Johnson's clothing line was "Catch Me"; however, the clothing line never caught on.[[37]](#cite_note-GlobeAndMail-37)

In a January 1, 2006 interview,[[38]](#cite_note-38) Johnson claimed that he was sabotaged by a "Mystery Man"[[39]](#cite_note-39) inside the doping control room immediately following the 100 metres final in Seoul. He also stated that 40% of people in the sports world are still taking drugs to improve their performance.

In August 2008, Johnson filed a $37 million lawsuit against the estate of his former lawyer Ed Futerman, claiming Futerman made unauthorized payments from his trust account to pay bills and 20 percent commissions to a hairdresser recruited by the lawyer to act as the sprinter's sports agent. In 2012, the lawsuit was dismissed by the Ontario Superior Court by summary judgment on the basis that "there were no genuine issues raised requiring a trial".[[40]](#cite_note-40)

At present, Johnson lives in [Markham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Markham,_Ontario "Markham, Ontario"), Ontario, and spends much of his time with his daughter and granddaughter. He also continues to coach, notably with [New Jersey Devils](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Jersey_Devils "New Jersey Devils") defenceman [P.K. Subban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P.K._Subban "P.K. Subban").[[41]](#cite_note-41) In 2010, he released his autobiography entitled *Seoul to Soul.*[[37]](#cite_note-GlobeAndMail-37) In the self-published book, Johnson reviews his childhood in Jamaica, and his early bout with [malaria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaria "Malaria"). A Canadian Press article described the book as "an unconventional sports autobiography."[[42]](#cite_note-42)

### Rivalry with Carl Lewis

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Rivalry with Carl Lewis")]

The duels between the two competitors reached immense popularity, fans all over the world watched the duels with excitement. They matched 17 times. Lewis won the first eight, then Johnson won seven out of nine races. In all these years only one short verbal exchange between them is known. They were very different in various aspects. They came from different countries; one from Canada, one from the USA. While Ben grew up poor, Carl's parents both went to college. Ben liked to party with his other rivals and had the reputation of a ladies' man; Carl on the other hand did not party often and was not as popular among the other athletes. Ben was incredible in the first 60 metres and had difficulties in the last 10 where Lewis was the fastest one. Carl benefited from his elegance and speed endurance whereas Johnson had impressive strength. He could bench press 165 kg, weighing only 72.[[43]](#cite_note-43)

## Advertising career

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Advertising career")]

In March 2006, television spots featuring Johnson advertising an [energy drink](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Energy_drink "Energy drink"), "[Cheetah Power Surge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_D'Angelo#Business_career "Frank D'Angelo")", started to receive some airtime. Some pundits questioned whether Johnson was an appropriate spokesperson for an all natural energy drink considering his history of steroid use.[[44]](#cite_note-44)[[45]](#cite_note-45) One ad is a mock interview between Johnson and [Frank D'Angelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_D'Angelo "Frank D'Angelo"), the president and chief executive of D'Angelo Brands, which makes the drink, in which he asks Johnson: "Ben, when you run, do you Cheetah?" "Absolutely," says Johnson. "I Cheetah all the time." The other commercial includes Johnson and a cheetah, the world's fastest land animal, and encourages viewers to "go ahead and Cheetah."

In May 2017, Johnson appeared in an advertising campaign for Australia's leading mobile bookmaker, [Sportsbet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sportsbet.com.au "Sportsbet.com.au"). The campaign launched Sportsbet's new Android app, with Johnson cheekily saying it "has tested positive for speed and power, again and again". The campaign tagline was "Putting the 'Roid in Android" and concluded with Johnson in the starters' block on a racing track, telling punters to "get on it!" The advertisement was pulled after complaints from various parties.[[46]](#cite_note-46)

## Documentaries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter)&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Documentaries")]

The [CBC Radio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CBC_Radio "CBC Radio") documentary series *[Rewind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rewind_(radio_program) "Rewind (radio program)")* broadcast an episode titled *Ben Johnson: A Hero Disgraced*[[47]](#cite_note-47) on September 19, 2013, for the 25th anniversary of the race, revealing 20 athletes tested positive for drugs but were cleared by the [IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOC "IOC") at the [1988 Seoul Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Seoul_Olympics "1988 Seoul Olympics"). An [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) official told the [CBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canadian_Broadcasting_Corporation "Canadian Broadcasting Corporation") that endocrine profiles done at those games indicated that 80 percent of the track and field athletes tested showed evidence of long-term steroid use, although few were banned or had their medals stripped.

In October 2012, [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN") and the BBC dual-financed a documentary entitled *9.79\**, which explores the doping scandal of Ben Johnson at the 1988 Summer Olympic 100 metre final.[[48]](#cite_note-48)[[49]](#cite_note-49)

In 2025, [Paramount+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount+ "Paramount+") and [GameTV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GameTV "GameTV") ordered a satirical docudrama miniseries on Johnson, *[Hate the Player: The Ben Johnson Story](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hate_the_Player:_The_Ben_Johnson_Story "Hate the Player: The Ben Johnson Story")*, from [Anthony Q. Farrell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Q._Farrell "Anthony Q. Farrell") and New Metric Media.[[50]](#cite_note-50)

## Summary: Ben Johnson (Canadian Sprinter)

This Wikipedia article covers the life and career of **Benjamin Sinclair Johnson Jr.** (born December 30, 1961), a Canadian former sprinter. He was once the world's fastest man, but his legacy is defined by a doping scandal.

### Key Career Highlights
- Born in Falmouth, Jamaica; emigrated to Canada in 1976.
- Trained by coach Charlie Francis at York University.
- **1984 Los Angeles Olympics:** Won bronze in the 100m and 4×100m relay.
- **1986:** Set a 60m world record (6.50s); won gold at the Commonwealth Games and Goodwill Games.
- **1987 World Championships (Rome):** Beat Carl Lewis and set a 100m world record of 9.83 seconds.
- **1988 Seoul Olympics:** Won the 100m final in a new world record of 9.79 seconds.

### Doping Scandal and Disqualification
- Three days after the 1988 Olympics, Johnson tested positive for the anabolic steroid **stanozolol** and was stripped of his gold medal and world record.
- He later admitted to using steroids since 1981. His 1987 world record was also rescinded.
- The scandal led to the **Dubin Inquiry** in Canada (1989), which investigated widespread drug use in sports.
- Johnson's coach, Charlie Francis, alleged that steroid use was rampant among top athletes, and that the 1988 100m final was "the dirtiest race in history" (only 2 of 8 runners remained clean throughout their careers).

### Comeback Attempts and Later Life
- After a suspension, he returned in 1991 but failed to qualify for the 1992 Olympics final.
- In 1993, he tested positive for excess testosterone and received a **lifetime ban** from the IAAF.
- In 1999, a Canadian adjudicator allowed an appeal on procedural grounds, but he failed another drug test that same year.
- He briefly trained Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi's son and Argentine footballer Diego Maradona.
- He has since lived in Ontario, Canada, continuing to coach and releasing an autobiography (*Seoul to Soul*) in 2010.
- He has maintained that he was sabotaged, alleging someone may have spiked his beer in the doping control room.

### Advertising and Documentaries
- Johnson appeared in commercials for "Cheetah Power Surge" energy drink (2006) and a Sportsbet campaign (2017).
- Documentaries about his life and the doping scandal include ESPN's *9.79\** (2012) and a satirical docudrama *Hate the Player: The Ben Johnson Story* (2025).

# [Ben Johnson doping scandal series coming to Paramount+ Canada](https://runningmagazine.ca/the-scene/ben-johnson-doping-scandal-series-coming-to-paramount-canada/ "Ben Johnson doping scandal series coming to Paramount+ Canada")

## The role of the disgraced sprinter will be played by John Wick: Chapter 4's Shamier Anderson

[Anne Francis](https://runningmagazine.ca/author/annefrancis/)Published June 19, 2025

![Ben Johnson](data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB3aWR0aD0iMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIxIiB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciPjwvc3ZnPg==)

Canadian Olympic Committee

A new six-episode drama series based on Canadian sprinter [**Ben Johnson**](https://runningmagazine.ca/the-scene/ben-johnson-thinks-doping-is-worse-than-30-years-ago/) and his dramatic downfall at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul is coming to Paramount+ Canada and GameTV in early 2026. Produced by Toronto’s New Metric Media and Bay Mills Studios, the series, to be titled *Hate the Player: The Ben Johnson Story,* will feature Canada’s own **Shamier Anderson** (who appeared in John Wick: Chapter 4) in the role of the disgraced sprinter. Principal photography is slated to begin Friday at Toronto’s Dark Slope Studios.

The show, which was commissioned by GameTV (which will also handle cable distribution in Canada) is [reported to take](https://deadline.com/2025/06/shamier-anderson-playing-ben-johnson-in-hate-the-player-paramount-1236436523/) a satirical view of the story, and is “inspired by extensive research conducted by Canadian author and journalist, **Mary Ormsby,”** whose book *World’s Fastest Man: The Incredible Life of Ben Johnson,* was published in 2024. (It was [reviewed](https://members.runningmagazine.ca/2024/06/reviews-41/) in the July/August 2024 issue of *Canadian Running.)*

> [New evidence suggests Ben Johnson’s 1988 Olympic lab report was tampered with](https://runningmagazine.ca/the-scene/ben-johnsons-1988-olympic-drug-test-was-tampered-with/)

Three days after winning gold in the 100m final in Seoul, Johnson was forced to give up his medal after testing positive for the banned steroid stanozolol, and his result was disqualified. This led to the Dubin Inquiry of 1989, which uncovered widespread doping among Canadian athletes.

[Anderson talked about](https://deadline.com/2025/06/shamier-anderson-playing-ben-johnson-in-hate-the-player-paramount-1236436523/) what the project means to him: “I grew up in Scarborough, where Ben trained, where his name still echoes. He was a hometown legend. Yes, complicated, but also someone people rooted for. Getting to do this alongside New Metric Media, who’ve been killing it in comedy, is a real honour, not just as an actor, but as an executive producer with my company, Bay Mills Studios.”

Anderson’s role in John Wick: Chapter 4 was Mr Nobody/The Tracker, and he appeared in the 2024 film, *The Luckiest Man in America.* The series is written by BAFTA-winning and Emmy-nominated writer **Anthony Q. Farrell**, whose credits also include *The Office* and *Run the Burbs*. Anderson started Bay Mills Studios along with his brother, **Stephan James.**

The series will be streamed exclusively in Canada by Paramount+ Canada

## Biography

Making his Olympic debut at Los Angeles 1984, and after false starting in the 100m final, Canada’s Ben Johnson won the bronze medal in 10.22 seconds, preventing an American sweep of the podium. In the 4x100m relay final, he won his second bronze medal of the Games along with Tony Sharpe, Desai Williams and Sterling Hinds. It was at Seoul 1988, where Johnson’s decade long rivalry with American Carl Lewis, which had been building for years, would come to a head. It was September 24, 1988 when Johnson became the first sprinter from Canada since Percy Williams at Amsterdam 1928 to win the 100m Olympic final lowering his own world record to 9.79 seconds. His status as Olympic champion would last 62 hours, and when he tested positive for the banned substance stanozolol (anabolic steroid), his gold medal and records were withdrawn and he was disqualified from the Games. After serving this drug suspension, Johnson returned to the Olympic theatre under immense global attention to run at Barcelona 1992 where he finished eighth in the 100m semi-final after stumbling out of the blocks, and was the lead-off runner for the 4x100m relay team that was disqualified in the semi-final.

Johnson, nicknamed “Big Ben”, first saw international success winning two silver medals at the 1982 Commonwealth Games. He would become a five-time Commonwealth Games medalist winning with all-time medal count of two gold, two silver and one bronze at Brisbane 1982 (100m and 4x100m relay silvers) and Edinburgh 1986 (100m and 4x100m relay gold, 200m bronze). Winning the 100m over Lewis in a world record of 9.83 seconds at the 1987 World Championships in Rome brought Johnson instant world-wide fame and lucrative marketing contracts but his subsequent positive drug test in 1988 wiped out both his title and his records. A two-time World Indoor champion over 60m in 1985 and 1987, Johnson was ultimately disqualified from the 1987 race after admitting in 1989 that he used performance enhancing drugs. His only appearance at the Pan American Games was in 1983 where he finished fifth in the 100m. 

Just months prior to the 1993 World Indoor Championships in his hometown of Toronto, Johnson won a 50m race in Grenoble, France, running 5.65 seconds (0.04 seconds off of the world record), tested positive for excessive testosterone, and was banned for life by the International Amateur Athletics Federation (IAAF).

Jamaican-born Johnson moved the Canada with his mother and three of his five siblings at the age of 14, leaving his father behind to continue working at the phone company. At 15, he was inspired by watching Montréal 1976 and was introduced by his brother to his one and only track coach, Charlie Francis, a three-time national 100m champion (1970, 1971, 1973) and Munich 1972 Olympian. Within four years, Johnson competed at the 1980 Pan American Junior Championships in Sudbury, meeting who would be his career rival, American Carl Lewis, for the first time. He finished sixth in the 100m and won a bronze medal in the 4x100m relay.

As a result of Johnson’s positive drug test at Seoul 1988, the federal government of Canada established a Commission of Inquiry to investigate the use of banned substances in Canadian sport, led by Chief Justice Charles Dubin. The Dubin Inquiry started in January 1989, went for 91 days, included 122 witnesses, with 46 athletes admitting to steroid use and costing the Canadian taxpayers $5 million. On June 12, 1989 Johnson was the last to testify and told the inquiry: “I lied. I lied and I was ashamed for my family, my friends, other Canadian athletes. I was just in a mess.” Time would prove that five of the other seven runners in the 100m final at Seoul 1988 were eventually caught cheating during their career.

After his track running days were over, Johnson continued to live in the Toronto area spending time with his daughter and grandchildren. He was involved in various business ventures and wrote his memoir “Seoul to Soul: Autobiography”. His celebrity status diminished in Canada but still shone bright in many other countries and travelled extensively making appearances. His father figure Charlie Francis died in 2010 at age 61 from non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In 1985, Johnson won the Norton Crowe Award for Male Athlete of the Year. In 1987, he won the Lou Marsh Trophy and Lionel Conacher Award, was named the Associated Press Athlete of the Year, and made a member of the Order of Canada. Johnson was inducted into the Canadian Olympic Hall of Fame in1988.

![](https://a3.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=%2Fredesign%2Fassets%2Fimg%2Ficons%2FESPN%2Dicon%2Dtennis.png&w=40&h=40&scale=crop&cquality=40&location=origin)

# Tennis

# Maria Sharapova suspended 2 years over positive doping test

![]()![](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/columnists/full/rovell_darren.png&h=80&w=80&scale=crop)
![Copy Link](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/i/content-reactions/check.png&h=80&w=80)

[Maria Sharapova](https://www.espn.com/sports/tennis/players/profile?playerId=399) was suspended for two years [by the International Tennis Federation on Wednesday](http://www.itftennis.com/news/231175.aspx), for testing positive for the banned substance meldonium.

She immediately responded by saying she would appeal the decision.

The ruling by an independent three-person panel appointed by the ITF said Sharapova, 29, did not intend to cheat but that she bore "sole responsibility'' and "very significant fault'' for the positive test.

"The ITF tribunal unanimously concluded that what I did was not intentional," Sharapova said in a statement. "The tribunal found that I did not seek treatment from my doctor for the purpose of obtaining a performance enhancing substance. The ITF spent tremendous amount of time and resources trying to prove I intentionally violated the anti-doping rules and the tribunal concluded I did not. You need to know that the ITF asked the tribunal to suspend me for four years -- the required suspension for an intentional violation -- and the tribunal rejected the ITF's position."

## [Why Maria Sharapova's career is far from over](/tennis/story/_/id/16046380/tennis-why-maria-sharapova-career-far-over) Greg Garber

![](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/photo/2016/0608/r90537_1296x1296_1-1.jpg&w=130&h=130&scale=crop&location=center)

## [Time is not on Maria Sharapova's side](/tennis/story/_/id/16048709/tennis-not-maria-sharapova-side) Peter Bodo

![](https://a.espncdn.com/combiner/i?img=/photo/2016/0311/r62371_1296x1296_1-1.jpg&w=130&h=130&scale=crop&location=center)

## [Sharapova case underscores holes in doping, anti-doping efforts](/tennis/story/_/id/16050173/tennis-doping-anti-doping-efforts-questioned-maria-sharapova-suspension) Bonnie D. Ford

The ITF, last month before the tribunal, asked for Sharapova to be suspended for four years, but the rules state that she could not be suspended for longer than two years if it was deemed that her use of the drug was not intentional.

"I cannot accept an unfairly harsh two-year suspension," Sharapova said. "The tribunal, whose members were selected by the ITF, agreed that I did not do anything intentionally wrong, yet they seek to keep me from playing tennis for two years."

The WTA issued a statement on the ruling, saying in part, "It is important at all times for players to be aware of the rules and to follow them. In this case, Maria has taken responsibility for her mistake from the outset. The WTA supports the process that the ITF and Maria have followed."

![]()

Sharapova and the Russian team had hoped she would be cleared in time to compete at the Olympics in Rio de Janeiro in August, but after the ruling, Russian Tennis Federation president Shamil Tarpischev told the Tass news agency that Ekaterina Makarova would replace her.

She was provisionally suspended by the ITF in March, when she announced she failed a doping test in January, at the Australian Open. Sharapova maintained that she was unaware that the drug she had been taking since 2006, mildronate, was also known as meldonium. That drug became a banned substance on the World Anti-Doping Agency's list as of Jan. 1.

Her lawyer, John Haggerty, said Sharapova took the substance after that date.

In addition to Sharapova's testing positive at the Australian Open, the ITF said she also failed a test for meldonium in an out-of-competition control in Moscow on Feb. 2.

"I am disappointed that the ITF tribunal gave Maria an unfairly harsh suspension because she is such a famous athlete and they wanted to make an example out of her," Haggerty said in a statement Wednesday, adding that he believes Sharapova's suspension will be reduced at her appeal.

Sharapova said in March she had started using the drug, which boosts blood and oxygen flow, under a doctor's guidance a decade ago because of irregular electrocardiogram results and a family history of heart issues and diabetes.

The governing body argued that Sharapova's records with the doctor ended in 2013, yet she continued to take the drug.

The appeal will be sent to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, where three judges will make the ruling. Both Sharapova and the ITF get to choose one of the judges. The decision will be binding.

By rule, Sharapova had to be suspended at least one year because she did not dispute that she took mildronate after Jan. 1, when it appeared on the banned list.

The sentence will be retroactive to the Australian Open, so if Sharapova's original suspension is kept, she will sit out through the 2018 Australian Open. That would mean she would be 31 years old when she competes in her next Grand Slam tournament.

A five-time major winner, Sharapova's last big win came at the 2014 French Open. She hasn't played since a quarterfinal loss to Serena Williams at the Australian Open and is ranked 26th this week.

The tribunal's ruling, as long as it's not reversed on appeal, could be worth a lot of money to Sharapova because of the finding that her use wasn't performance-enhancing. When she announced her positive test, her endorsement deals with Nike and Porsche were suspended.

Nike said in a statement Wednesday that it had lifted her suspension based on ITF's findings, but did not know whether it planned to use her soon. "Based on the decision of the ITF and their factual findings," the statement said, in part, "We hope to see Maria back on court and will continue to partner with her."

One of her other endorsers, Head, said Wednesday it will continue to stand by Sharapova, calling the ITA's decision flawed.

Evian also has continued using the tennis star, while watchmaker Tag Heuer elected not to renew its deal at the start of this year and Avon, the manufacturer of beauty and personal care products, announced it would not extend a partnership that was set to expire.

Despite Sharapova being off the court, the narrative of her suspension could affect her own brand; her "Sugarpova" line of gummy candy and most recently chocolate have gained worldwide distribution.

*The Associated Press contributed to this report.*

# What is meldonium and why did Maria Sharapova take it?

This article is more than 10 years old

Meldonium is also known as mildronate, it increases exercise capacity in athletes and Sharapova claimed she had been taking the drug for 10 years because of a magnesium deficiency and family history of diabetes

Maria Sharapova was on Wednesday banned from tennis for two years after [failing a drugs test](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/mar/07/maria-sharapova-failed-drugs-test-australian-open-2016-tennis) at this year’s Australian Open, once again putting meldonium under the spotlight.

Meldonium is also known as mildronate, the name by which Sharapova knew the drug, having taken it since 2006.

[Maria Sharapova doping ban reduced to 15 months as French Open return likely

Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/oct/04/maria-sharapova-doping-ban-reduced-french-open-return)

But what do we know about the substance, why was the Russian taking it and why was it banned only this year?

Meldonium is used to treat ischaemia: a lack of blood flow to parts of the body, particularly in cases of angina or heart failure.

[It is manufactured in Latvia](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/mar/08/meldonium-treatment-four-to-six-weeks-maria-sharapova) and only distributed in Baltic countries and Russia. It is not approved by the Food and Drug Administration for use in the United States and is not authorised in the rest of Europe.

It increases blood flow, which improves exercise capacity in athletes.

Wada found “evidence of its use by athletes with the intention of enhancing performance” by virtue of carrying more oxygen to muscle tissue.

The decision to add meldonium to the banned list was approved on 16 September 2015, and it came into effect on 1 January 2016. Wada had spent the previous year monitoring the drug before adding it to the banned list.

The drug was name-checked in the latest investigative documentary on Russian doping reforms by the German Hajo Seppelt [on Sunday](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2016/mar/06/iaaf-russia-athletes-banned). The documentary referred to a 2015 study in which 17% of Russian athletes (724 of 4,316) tested were found to have meldonium in their system. A global study found 2.2% of athletes had it in their system.

[L’Equipe reported](http://www.lequipe.fr/Tennis/Actualites/Qu-est-ce-que-le-meldonium-la-substance-nouvellement-interdite-detectee-chez-maria-sharapova/641184) that the scientific advisor to the French Agency Against Doping (AFLD), Professor Xavier Bigard, said in interviews with athletes at last year’s European Games in Baku that a wide proportion of athletes admitted taking meldonium.

[Maria Sharapova’s aura will forever bear a blemish amid the doubts | Richard Williams

Read more](https://www.theguardian.com/sport/blog/2016/mar/11/maria-sharapova-aura-blemish-doubts-tennis)

It is classed as an S4 substance under the Wada code, which addresses hormone and metabolic modulators.

The standard ban under the World Anti-Doping Code is four years.

A memo was sent out to athletes by Russia’s anti-doping agency last September informing them of the decision to ban its use.
