The following is a  **list of Major League Baseball players named in the [Mitchell Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitchell_Report "Mitchell Report")**,[[1]](#cite_note-abc-list-1)[[2]](#cite_note-espn-list-2)[[3]](#cite_note-wcbs-list-3)[[4]](#cite_note-chron-list-4)[[5]](#cite_note-Lackey-5) including active and former [Major League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") players as well as [free agents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_agent "Free agent"). The Report is the result of former [US Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Senator "US Senator") [George J. Mitchell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_J._Mitchell "George J. Mitchell")'s ([D](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Party_(United_States) "Democratic Party (United States)")–[ME](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maine "Maine")) 20-month investigation into [performance-enhancing drug use](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_(sport) "Doping (sport)") in [Major League Baseball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_League_Baseball "Major League Baseball") (MLB) released on December 13, 2007. Inclusion on the list does not necessarily mean the player was involved in illegal activity. In some instances, insufficient evidence was provided to draw a conclusion, and some players were mentioned in other contexts.

The Mitchell Report also stated that interviews were requested of five MLB players who had spoken out publicly on the steroid issue. Of these players, only one, [Frank Thomas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Thomas "Frank Thomas"), was willing to be interviewed. The Mitchell Report stated that there was no evidence that any of these five had used performance-enhancing drugs. [Curt Schilling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curt_Schilling "Curt Schilling"), one of the four players who declined to interview with Mitchell, explained that he denied Mitchell's request because he "would have nothing to offer" Mitchell's investigation "other than personal opinion and hypotheticals."[[6]](#cite_note-NYT_2007-12-15-6)

[Jason Giambi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jason_Giambi "Jason Giambi") was required to interview with Mitchell and his investigators by Commissioner [Bud Selig](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bud_Selig "Bud Selig") under threat of discipline. This stemmed from Giambi's ongoing involvement with the [BALCO investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BALCO_scandal "BALCO scandal") and statements he had given to the media.

The Report is the result of former US Senator George J. Mitchell's (D–ME) 20-month investigation into performance-enhancing drug use in Major League Baseball (MLB) released on December 13, 2007.", "Inclusion on the list does not necessarily mean the player was involved in illegal activity. In some instances, insufficient evidence was provided to draw a conclusion, and some players were mentioned in other contexts.", "The Mitchell Report also stated that interviews were requested of five MLB players who had spoken out publicly on the steroid issue. Of these players, only one, Frank Thomas, was willing to be interviewed.", "On December 18, Clemens (through his agent) denied taking steroids, human growth hormone, or any other banned substance(s) in his life. He stated that his opinion of such substances were 'a dangerous and destructive shortcut that no athlete should ever take.'", "After the Mitchell Report was made public, Pettitte released a statement admitting his use of human growth hormone on two occasions in 2002, which he says was only intended to accelerate his recovery from an elbow injury."
args.summary:
This Wikipedia article is a list of Major League Baseball players named in the Mitchell Report, the result of former US Senator George J. Mitchell's 20-month investigation into performance-enhancing drug use in MLB, released on December 13, 2007. Inclusion does not necessarily mean the player was involved in illegal activity, as insufficient evidence existed in some cases.

The page is organized into categories:

1. **Implicated in the BALCO Scandal (9 players)**: Includes Barry Bonds, Jason Giambi, Gary Sheffield, Benito Santiago, Jeremy Giambi, Marvin Benard, Bobby Estalella, Armando Ríos, and Randy Velarde. Key details include Bonds' alleged admission to using substances for sleeping/arthritis, Jason Giambi testing positive for Deca-Durabolin, and Sheffield's FedEx receipt to BALCO.

2. **Identified as clients of Kirk Radomski (53 players)**: Includes Roger Clemens, Andy Pettitte, Eric Gagné, Paul Lo Duca, David Justice, Chuck Knoblauch, Kevin Brown, Jason Grimsley, and others. Players like Clemens were alleged to have used HGH, Deca-Durabolin, Winstrol, and Sustanon. Clemens denied the allegations and filed a defamation suit against trainer Brian McNamee. Pettitte admitted using HGH in 2002 to recover from an elbow injury. Many players admitted to purchasing HGH and steroids from Radomski, often for injury recovery.

The report also notes that five MLB players who had spoken out on steroids were requested for interviews, but only Frank Thomas agreed to be interviewed. Jason Giambi was required to interview under threat of discipline from Commissioner Bud Selig due to his involvement in the BALCO investigation.

[The Olympic flag.](https://cdn.britannica.com/43/226243-050-881B1638/Olympic-flag.jpg)Drug testing at the Olympics began in 1968.(more)

Drug testing at the [Olympics](https://www.britannica.com/sports/Olympic-Games) began in 1968. As of the[2020 Summer Games in Tokyo](https://www.britannica.com/event/Tokyo-2020-Olympic-Games), there had been 442 positive doping tests, resulting in the loss of 173 medals (57 gold, 66 silver, and 50 bronze) over 28 Games in 52 years.

Russian athletes have most often tested positive, with 133 positive doping results, and have had the most medals stripped from athletes at 63 total (17 gold, 34 silver, and 12 bronze). The most positive tests are found in athletics (track and field), with 172 positive tests and 59 lost medals (22 gold, 23 silver, and 14 bronze).

Turinabol, an androgenic [anabolic steroid](https://www.britannica.com/science/anabolic-steroid), is the drug most associated with positive doping tests, showing up in 65 tests by itself and in 9 drug cocktails for another 35 positive tests. All in all, positive results showing turinabol resulted in the loss of 54 medals (8 gold, 24 silver, and 22 bronze).

Below, explore positive doping results by Games,country,sport, and drug(s) or drug offense. [[41]](https://www.britannica.com/procon/sports-and-drugs-debate/Assessment-Quiz#pcref-2256827-41)

args.summary: This Britannica ProCon.org article presents a comprehensive overview of doping in sports, focusing on Olympic doping cases. It includes the pros and cons of performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs), a detailed historical timeline from ancient Greece (776 BCE) to 2026, and an extensive list of banned substances and methods. Key data: As of the 2020 Tokyo Games, there were 442 positive doping tests across 28 Games (52 years), resulting in 173 lost medals. Russian athletes lead with 133 positive tests and 63 stripped medals. Athletics (track and field) has the most positive tests (172). Turinabol is the most common drug linked to positive tests (65). The article provides tables of doping cases by Games (from 1968 to 2024), by country, and by sport. Notable recent events include the 2024 Chinese doping scandal, Jannik Sinner's 2025 ban, and the 2026 inaugural Enhanced Games.

The use of [performance-enhancing drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performance-enhancing_substance "Performance-enhancing substance") ([doping in sport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_sport "Doping in sport")) is prohibited within the sport of [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics"). Athletes who are found to have used such banned substances, whether through a positive drugs test, the [biological passport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_passport "Biological passport") system, an investigation or public admission, may receive a competition [ban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ban_(law) "Ban (law)") for a length of time which reflects the severity of the infraction. Athletes who are found to have banned substances in their possession, or who tamper with or refuse to submit to drug testing can also receive bans from the sport. Competitive bans may also be given to athletes who test positive for prohibited [recreational drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Recreational_drug_use "Recreational drug use") or stimulants with little performance-enhancing effect for competitors in athletics. The sports body responsible for determining which substances are banned in athletics is the [World Anti-Doping Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Anti-Doping_Agency "World Anti-Doping Agency") (WADA).

Typically, any athlete who tests positive for banned substances after having served a previous ban receives a lifetime ban from the sport of athletics. Many high-profile sportspeople to receive doping bans have come from the sport of athletics, with significant past cases concerning [Ben Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ben_Johnson_(Canadian_sprinter) "Ben Johnson (Canadian sprinter)"), [Marion Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Jones "Marion Jones") and [Tim Montgomery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_Montgomery "Tim Montgomery"). Furthermore, a number of athletes who underwent state-sponsored [doping programmes in East Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_East_Germany "Doping in East Germany") and the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_Russia#Soviet_era "Doping in Russia") between the 1950s and 1980s were competitors in athletics, but the quality of the international anti-doping work was so poor that only one East German athlete ever tested positive.[[1]](#cite_note-Berendonk-1) Following allegations of state-sponsored [doping in Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doping_in_Russia "Doping in Russia"), the IAAF suspended the country's athletes from competition, including the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").

The page explains that performance-enhancing drug use is prohibited in athletics, with the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) determining banned substances. Athletes found violating rules through positive tests, biological passport anomalies, investigations, or public admissions receive competition bans, with repeat offenders typically receiving lifetime bans.

The article notes significant historical cases involving Ben Johnson, Marion Jones, and Tim Montgomery, as well as state-sponsored doping programs in East Germany and the Soviet Union. It also references the Russian doping scandal that led to the IAAF suspending Russian athletes from competition including the 2016 Summer Olympics.

The bulk of the page consists of an extensive table listing hundreds of doping cases alphabetically by athlete name, including details such as: athlete name, country, event, date of violation, banned substance(s) or anti-doping rule violation, sanction length, and reference citations. The table covers cases from the 1970s through 2016, spanning athletes from numerous countries across all athletic disciplines (sprinting, middle/long distance, throwing events, jumping events, race walking, etc.). Sanctions range from public warnings to lifetime bans, with common substances including anabolic steroids (e.g., Stanozolol, Metenolone, Nandrolone), stimulants (Ephedrine, Cannabis), EPO, masking agents, and biological passport violations.

This summary will be used by a downstream research agent, so it's crucial to maintain the key details without losing essential information.

Here is the raw content of the webpage:

<webpage_content>
By: Sara Kettler

[Cold War](/topics/cold-war)

# 9 Doping Scandals That Changed Sports

Athletes have always been driven to win, but the advent of performance-enhancing drugs has resulted in stripped titles, ban from sports and more.

[![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_auto,ar_1,w_3840,h_3840,g_face/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/Kettler_Sara_hxj99i?_a=BAVMn6DY0)Sara Kettler](/authors/sara-kettler)

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_2,w_3840,h_1920,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-53451999?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

JOEL SAGET/AFP via Getty Images

Published: May 26, 2021Last Updated: February 18, 2025

Throughout history, athletes have been willing to ingest just about anything to improve their performance on the field. Some ancient Greeks [turned to figs](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19467612/), while others [used mushrooms](https://foreignpolicy.com/2016/08/03/everything-bad-about-rio-olympics-worse-ancient-greece-doping-cheating-zika/), and ancient Egyptians believed that [ground mule hooves](https://www.pbs.org/wnet/secrets/the-dangers-of-doping/56/) could boost their athletic prowess. In 1807, an endurance walker in Britain [took laudanum](https://books.google.com/books?id=lMMYN0jY2u8C&pg=PA16) to stay awake around the clock in a competition.

## 10 Amazing Ancient Olympic Facts

From naked athletes to foot-only races, these are 10 surprising facts you didn’t know about the ancient Olympics.

9:30m watch

A runner in the 1904 Olympic marathon imbibed a mixture of [strychnine, raw eggs and brandy](https://books.google.com/books?id=to0WOYRzlZIC&pg=PA8) and won his race (though he barely survived and quickly quit the sport). And in the 1930s an English football club bragged about dosing its players with [monkey gland extract](https://books.google.com/books?id=TeAUDAAAQBAJ&pg=PA15).

In recent times, however, performance-enhancing substances consist of steroids, human growth hormone and blood-boosting erythropoietin, and taking them courts both danger and censure. Doping in the 20th and 21st centuries has produced tainted victories and infamous scandals like these:

1.

## 1967: Cyclist Tom Simpson dies after Tour de France

British cyclist Tom Simpson passed away during the Tour de France on July 13, 1967, as he pedaled up Mont Ventoux on an extremely hot day. Simpson's cause of death was listed as a heart attack due to dehydration. However, there were tubes of amphetamines in his jersey and an autopsy found traces of amphetamines.

An [official report](https://books.google.com/books?id=to0WOYRzlZIC&pg=PA33) related that the drugs Simpson took made it possible for him to push himself into an overworked and dehydrated state. His death led to an International Cycling Union ban on the use of performance-enhancing drugs in cycling.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_0.9813084112149533,w_3840,h_3912,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-513640935?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Cyclist Tommy Simpson before the first stage of the Tour de France on June 21, 1966, in Nancy, France.

Getty Images

2.

## 1970s and '80s: German government forces its athletes to use steroids

In the 1970s and '80s, the East German government decided to dose its athletes with performance-enhancing drugs, most notably steroids, in the belief that sports wins would demonstrate the superiority of communism. Athletes noticed their bodies changing, yet had little choice but to go along in an authoritarian system. Some swimmers even [said](https://books.google.com/books?id=yCzbk7F8DGgC&pg=PA98) to each other, "You eat the pills, or you die."

At the 1976 Olympics in Montreal, the East German women's swim team won 11 gold medals out of a possible 13, contributing to an overall haul of 40 gold medals. Competitors and observers suspectedthe East Germans were taking steroids, but state resources were used to continue and cover up the doping program. All in all, at least 9,000 athletes were given performance-enhancing drugs. Following German reunification in 1990, some perpetrators of the doping scheme were tried and found guilty. However, this didn't erase the price paid by athletes, many of whom had been left with [lifelong health problems](https://www.dw.com/en/east-germanys-doping-program-casts-long-shadow-over-victims/a-5968383), including heart disease, infertility and cancer.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-52236481?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Swimmers recieve their medals after the women’s 400 metres freestyle event at the Montreal Olympics, July 1976. Left to right: Shirley Babashoff of the U.S.A. (silver), Petra Thumer of East Germany (gold) and Shannon Smith of Canada (bronze).

Keystone/Hulton Archive/Getty Images

3.

## 1988: Track star Ben Johnson tests positive for steroids

When Canadian track star Ben Johnson won gold in the 100m at the Olympic Games in Seoul, South Korea on September 24, 1988, he not only established a new world record but also defeated his American rival, Carl Lewis. Then Johnson tested positive for the steroid stanozolol. In the face of this evidence, he returned his gold medal, which then went to Lewis.

Johnson had fame and million-dollar promotional deals before his fortunes reversed soon after his win. Yet his downfall helped open the world's eyes to the fact that doping, [previously seen as a Communist bloc](https://www.cbc.ca/sportslongform/entry/ben-johnson-vs-carl-lewis-the-race-and-the-disgrace) issue, was happening throughout athletics.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-516121450?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Ben Johnson crosses the finish line to win the Olympic 100m final in a world record 9.79 seconds on September 24, 1988, at Seoul Olympic Stadium.

ROMEO GACAD/AFP via Getty Images

4.

## 1994: Diego Maradona's ephedrine use eliminates the soccer player from the World Cup

Argentinian soccer player Diego Maradona, who'd led his team to victory in 1986's World Cup, tested positive for five different variants of ephedrine at the 1994 World Cup. Though he'd been suspended for 15 months in 1991-92 due to cocaine use, Maradona had [seemed to be making a comeback](https://www.nytimes.com/1994/07/01/sports/world-cup-94-after-second-test-maradona-is-out-of-world-cup.html): he'd lost 26 pounds to get ready for the tournament and had demonstrated his continued abilities with a goal and an assist in the first round.

Instead of continuing to represent his home country, Maradona made news for being tossed out of the competition. His career lasted a few more years, but he never played for Argentina again.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-79041504?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Fans hold up a sign at the 1994 World Cup finals calling for the return of Diego Maradona after he was banned for failing a drug test.

Bob Thomas Sports Photography via Getty Images

5.

## 1998: The Festina cycling team is caught doping during the Tour de France

During a border search in Lille, a French town near Belgium, the Festina cycling team's masseur was found to be transporting amphetamines, erythropoietin and steroids, all performance-enhancing substances. Police searches, raids and arrests were set in motion by this discovery, even as the Festina team began to compete in 1998's Tour de France.

After days of police interrogation, the team's manager and doctor [admitted](https://www.irishtimes.com/sport/chronicle-of-a-sport-in-turmoil-the-last-12-months-1.202752) to the Festina team's doping program. The team ended up being expelled from the race. The scandal became [one of the factors](https://books.google.com/books?id=to0WOYRzlZIC&pg=PR9) in the creation of the [World Anti-Doping Agency](https://www.wada-ama.org/) in 1999.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-543763336?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

French cyclist Richard Virenque after being accused of taking performance-enhancing drugs, July 17, 1998.

Stephane Ruet/Sygma via Getty Images

6.

## 2003: The BALCO scandal begins

In October 2003, the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency announced that the designer steroid tetrahydrogestrinone (THG), which had been undetectable to tests, was used by a number of athletes. It was a tipster—later revealed to be the former coach of track star Marion Jones—who had informed investigators earlier in the year about the existence of THG, and that the source was the Bay Area Laboratory Co-operative, called BALCO, and its founder, Victor Conte.

In 2007, Jones [admitted](https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=18028502) to using steroids. She surrendered the five medals—three gold and two bronze—she'd been awarded at the 2000 Olympics in Sydney, Australia. In 2008, she was sentenced to six months in prison for lying to federal investigators about her steroid use. San Francisco Giants player Barry Bonds, who broke baseball's all-time home run record in 2007, was another BALCO client. He testified he never knowingly took steroids, but this denial was countered by [reporting](https://www.espn.com/mlb/news/story?id=3113127) that Bonds had used multiple performance-enhancing drugs.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-2552745?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Barry Bonds warms up prior to batting during a game against the Houston Astros at Minute Maid Park in Houston, Texas on September 23, 2003.

Jamie Squire/Getty Images

7.

## 2012: Cyclist Lance Armstrong is stripped of his Tour de France titles

American cyclist Lance Armstrong won seven Tour de France titles in a row from 1999 to 2005. His wins made him famous, and the fact that he accomplished this as a cancer survivor earned him even more plaudits.

Along the way, [questions were asked](https://www.espn.com/olympics/cycling/story/_/id/29177227/line-lance-armstrong-career-successes-doping-allegations-final-collapse) about his possible use of performance-enhancing drugs, but no charges stuck. Then in 2010, Floyd Landis, a former teammate who'd been involved in his own doping scandal, accused Armstrong of doping.

In 2012, the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency [charged](https://www.usada.org/sanction/lance-armstrong-receives-lifetime-ban-and-disqualification-of-competitive-results-for-doping-violations-stemming-from-his-involvement-in-the-united-states-postal-service-pro-cycling-team-doping-conspi/) Armstrong with the use of performance-enhancing drugs. Armstrong ultimately didn't contest the charges, which resulted in the loss of his Tour de France titles and a ban from the sport of cycling. The agency released a report in October [calling](https://www.cnn.com/2012/10/10/sport/armstrong-doping-investigation/index.html) Armstrong part of "the most sophisticated, professionalized and successful doping program that sport has ever seen." In January 2013, Armstrong [confessed](https://www.espn.com/olympics/cycling/story/_/id/29177227/line-lance-armstrong-career-successes-doping-allegations-final-collapse) to Oprah Winfrey that he'd been doping for all of his Tour de France wins.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-102578667?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Lance Armstrong signs autographs following training on July 2, 2010, in Rotterdam, Netherlands.

Spencer Platt/Getty Images

## 2013: The Biogenesis scandal reveals doping in the MLB

In January 2013, [news broke](https://mlb.nbcsports.com/2019/12/27/top-25-baseball-stories-of-the-decade-no-8-biogenesis-scandal/) that Biogenesis, a Florida-based rejuvenation clinic, had been supplying several Major League Baseball players with human growth hormone and other performance-enhancing drugs. The story, set in motion by a [clinic employee with an axe to grind](https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/mlb/2014/08/05/biogenesis-anniversary-alex-rodriguez-ryan-braun-peds-tony-bosch-porter-fischer/13593357/), revealed that doping was still a problem for baseball.

MLB investigated and proceeded to suspend more than a dozen players. Most were out for 50 games, while right fielder Ryan Braun received a 65-game suspension and Yankees star Alex Rodriguez was suspended for 211 games (this was reduced to 162 games on appeal). Though Rodriguez initially protested his innocence, he [admitted](https://www.miamiherald.com/sports/mlb/article3578762.html) his doping to federal investigators, in exchange for immunity from prosecution. The scandal resulted in MLB promising to institute tougher penalties and more frequent testing.

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/aenetworks/image/upload/c_fill,ar_1.7777777777777777,w_3840,h_2158,g_auto/dpr_auto/f_auto/q_auto:eco/v1/gettyimages-526537070?_a=BAVMn6DY0)

Alex Rodriguez addresses the media after playing a minor league game for the Trenton Thunder in Trenton, New Jersey on August 3, 2013.

Mark Makela/Corbis via Getty Images

[## 2021 and 2022: Russia's Olympic ban for state-sponsored doping](/videos/the-olympic-games-fast-facts)

In 2016, the former head of an anti-doping laboratory in Moscow [blew the whistle](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/05/13/sports/russia-doping-sochi-olympics-2014.html) on a state-run initiative to provide Russian athletes with performance-enhancing drugs, and to hide that use, at the 2014 Olympic Games in Sochi, Russia. He described a cover-up that involved the intelligence service accessing "tamper-proof" bottles in order to replace urine from doping Russian athletes with safe-to-test samples. The World Anti-Doping Agency commissioned an investigation that [found evidence](https://www.bbc.com/sport/36823453) of this elaborate scheme.

In December 2019, after receiving [manipulated test results](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/12/09/sports/russia-doping-ban.html) from the Moscow lab, the World Anti-Doping Agency imposed a four-year ban on Russia for the Olympic Games and world championship sporting events. This was reduced to a two-year ban by the Court of Arbitration for Sport in 2020. Russian athletes were able to compete at the 2021 and 2022 Olympic Games, but not under the Russian flag or with their country's anthem.

This article from HISTORY.com, authored by Sara Kettler (published May 26, 2021, updated February 18, 2025), documents nine major doping scandals that have changed sports throughout history. It begins by noting that athletes have used performance-enhancing substances since ancient times, but modern doping involves steroids, human growth hormone, and erythropoietin. The nine scandals covered are:

1. **1967: Tom Simpson's death** — British cyclist died during the Tour de France after taking amphetamines, leading to the International Cycling Union's ban on performance-enhancing drugs.

2. **1970s-'80s: East German state-sponsored doping** — The East German government forced at least 9,000 athletes to use steroids; women's swim team won 11 of 13 gold medals at the 1976 Olympics. Perpetrators were later tried after reunification, but many athletes suffered lifelong health issues.

3. **1988: Ben Johnson** — Canadian sprinter tested positive for stanozolol after winning Olympic gold in the 100m; returned his medal to Carl Lewis and exposed doping as a widespread issue beyond the Communist bloc.

4. **1994: Diego Maradona** — Soccer star tested positive for ephedrine at the World Cup and was expelled; he never played for Argentina again.

5. **1998: Festina cycling team** — Team masseur was caught with doping substances at the Tour de France; the scandal contributed to the creation of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) in 1999.

6. **2003: BALCO scandal** — U.S. lab supplied undetectable designer steroid THG to athletes including Marion Jones (who surrendered five Olympic medals and served prison time) and Barry Bonds.

7. **2012: Lance Armstrong** — Stripped of seven Tour de France titles and banned for life after USADA called his program "the most sophisticated... doping program that sport has ever seen"; he confessed to Oprah in 2013.

8. **2013: Biogenesis scandal** — Florida clinic supplied MLB players with HGH and PEDs; over a dozen players suspended, including Alex Rodriguez (162 games) and Ryan Braun (65 games).

9. **2021-2022: Russia's Olympic ban** — State-sponsored doping scheme at the 2014 Sochi Olympics led to a two-year ban from the Court of Arbitration for Sport; Russian athletes competed but not under their flag or anthem.

<webpage_content>
# [Endurance Essentials](/)

# Altitude Simulation

### Part 6 of the Highs & Lows of Altitude

[john hellemans](https://substack.com/@johnhellemans)

You can access the series so far [here](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/88878316/altitude-with-john-hellemans):

* [Introduction](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/the-highs-and-lows-of-altitude-training)
* [Oxygen Dynamics](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/oxygen-dynamics)
* [Altitude Adaptation, Health & Ability To Train](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/altitude-adaptation-health-and-ability)
* [Conventional Altitude](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/conventional-altitude-training)

  + [Which Altitude To Choose](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/136312606/the-best-altitude-to-choose)
  + [How To Train](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/136312606/training-at-altitude)
  + [Where To Go](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/136312606/where-to-go)
  + [Monitoring & Using Lactate](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/136312606/monitoring)
  + [What To Expect Post-Altitude](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/136312606/performance-testing-and-tracking)
* [More On Natural Altitude](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/more-on-natural-altitude)

  + [Live High - Train Low](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/137129802/live-high-train-low)
  + [Live High - Train High & Low](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/137129802/live-high-train-high-and-low)
  + [Responders vs Non-Responders](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/137129802/responders-vs-non-responders)

---

Today we discuss Altitude Simulation, specifically:

* Altitude Houses
* Breath-holding (hypercapnic hypoxia)
* Altitude Tents (normobaric hypoxia)

Part Two will discuss Intermittent Hypoxic Exposure and Training.

---

### Altitude Houses

[Altitude Sport Hotel Pokljuka](https://hotelpokljuka.si/en/) in Slovenia, opened in 2017

For altitude training to be effective, a minimum of two to three weeks of altitude exposure is required, as it takes that long for the desired adaptations to take effect. Conventional altitude training (living and training in the mountains) is expensive unless you live there. Altitude simulation has come to the rescue.  The Scandinavians experimented in the early 1990s with their seemingly effective (but very expensive) altitude houses, built at sea level, for their cross-country skiers. The Finnish scientist Heikki Rusko is often credited with inventing the ‘altitude house’. Finland does not have natural high altitudes, so he sought easily accessible alternatives. Perhaps it was no coincidence that Norway and Finland were leading the way in developing alternative ways of increasing red blood cell production. At the time, rumours were rife that these were also the countries, together with Italy, which had extensively experimented with blood doping and E.P.O. to benefit their distance runners, cyclists and cross-country skiers since the mid-sixties. First, in 1985, blood doping was banned by the I.O.C., followed by erythropoietin (EPO) in 1990. It makes sense that scientists doubled their efforts in trying to find ways to maximise the performance-enhancing benefits of altitude training, which came closest to mimicking the effects of blood doping and EPO.

In 1994, the Winter Olympics were planned for Lillehammer, Norway. Much was at stake for the Scandinavian countries, with fierce competition regarding their rankings on the overall medal tally. Cross-country skiing is for these countries what American Football is in America, ice-speed skating in the Netherlands, cycling in Belgium and rugby in New Zealand.  Rusko came up with the idea of diluting oxygen in the air by replacing it with nitrogen, resulting in a low-oxygen (hypoxic) environment. The beauty of this method is that the exact altitude can be easily controlled and changed, and athletes can train indoors at altitude or outside at sea level. The Norwegians experimented with altitude chambers around the same time. They lowered oxygen levels in altitude chambers and houses by reducing the air pressure inside, mimicking the altitude environment. This results in a hypobaric (low pressure) hypoxic environment, while Rusko’s nitrogen house creates normobaric (sea level pressure) hypoxia.

Ironically, in 2003, altitude simulation methods were banned by the Governments of Norway and Italy. They based their decision on a paper published by Baker and Hopkins (1998), which suggested that hypoxic training gave athletes an unfair technological advantage and was dangerous if the training was not planned and monitored by an expert in hypoxic training. It was not made illegal, however, to travel to natural altitude to gain the benefits of hypoxia. As far as I know, the ban still exists in Italy but was lifted in Norway as recently as 2021. How the ban is monitored is a mystery to me, as the physiological changes brought about by altitude simulation are generally a lot more subtle and with significant individual variation compared to the use of blood doping and pharmacologically enhanced red blood cell production.

Today, normobaric chambers are more common in commercial and research settings due to their ease of use and lower operation cost than hypobaric chambers. They are widely used in sports training facilities, universities, and research laboratories. Hypobaric chambers are less common and are usually found in specialised research institutions, military facilities, and certain high-performance sports training centres where precise altitude simulations are required.

The discussion around which of the two is more effective for sports performance enhancement, hypobaric hypoxia or normobaric hypoxia, has not yet been resolved. Both induce physiological responses related to reduced oxygen availability, but the additional changes in atmospheric pressure in hypobaric hypoxia can possibly lead to more complex adaptations in the body. My own sense is that hypobaric hypoxia, which mimics the natural altitude conditions most closely, is likely to have additional benefits compared to the more widely used normobaric methods of altitude simulation. Science might be able to give us a more definite answer in the future.

Hypobaric hypoxic chambers are mainly used for military training and research.

The Americans developed more affordable altitude tents for individual use around the mid-nineties (below). They allow the athlete to sleep at altitude in their home and train at sea level. Altitude tents are based on the normobaric hypoxia method, where oxygen is extracted from the air by a ‘hypoxicator’ and replaced by nitrogen.

Although altitude houses and tents were considered new to most Western countries, altitude simulation existed well before that in Eastern Europe and Russia.  The first reports come from before the Second World War when Russian pilots pre-acclimatised with intermittent hypoxic exposure to prepare for their (open cockpit) flights at altitude. In the sixties, Eastern European countries developed special underground hypobaric chambers to enhance athletic performance. Since then, we have discovered that this was more likely to have been a smoke screen to hide more sinister and powerful (pharmacological) means to enhance performance. Only with the fall of the Iron Curtain did the technology involved with intermittent hypoxic exposure become more widely available to the West. Athletes have not only used intermittent hypoxic exposure and training to prepare for competition and mountaineers to go to altitude, but it has also been applied in the medical field to treat various chronic conditions. The next article will be devoted to Intermittent Hypoxic Exposure and Training.

---

### Breath-Holding

Breath-holding, also known as apnoea training, is a form of hypoxic training that involves voluntarily holding one's breath for extended periods. This practice is common among free divers, underwater swimmers, and athletes seeking to enhance their lung capacity and tolerance to hypoxia (low oxygen levels). While free divers and underwater swimmers practice active breath-holding on dry land while stationary, endurance athletes often incorporate some dynamic breath-holding during their training. It is more commonly practised by swimmers, including triathletes, as the rhythmic breathing pattern during the swimming motion leads itself well to incorporate breath-holding exercises. This is done by doing exercises where you breathe every so many strokes, extending the breath-holding over time. Doing lengths of underwater swimming is another exercise which can easily be incorporated into a swim session.  The result of these exercises is temporary hypoxia. The accompanying drop in SpO2 results over time in adaptations similar to those of altitude training but of a lesser magnitude. An added bonus is that the practice improves lung capacity and respiratory muscle strength. Like any conditioning, it must be done regularly to benefit you. If you incorporate some controlled breath-holding exercises in three or four swim sessions per week, it is likely to provide you with some benefits.

Breath-holding by breathing every so-many strokes

Breath-holding needs to be practised with caution and is best done under supervision as if done to the extreme, it can result in blackouts due to a combination of hypoxia and carbon dioxide build-up.

---

### The Altitude Tent

The altitude tent (photo above) is a small, enclosed structure. The tent fits over a regular bed, creating a sealed environment around the sleeping area. Outside the tent is a hypoxicator where oxygen is removed from the outside air and replaced by nitrogen.

Altitude tents have adjustable settings to control the oxygen concentration inside the tent, mimicking specific elevations as per Table 1.

As with natural altitude training, athletes must sleep in the tent for two to three weeks to generate worthwhile physiological adaptations. Short-term adaptations have been measured within 3 hours of exposure to altitude air in this manner. Still, scientists generally recommend that to achieve meaningful results, you must spend at least 12-14 hours per day in a hypoxic environment comparable with at least 2400 meters of altitude. This is achieved by sleeping in the tent and spending some time during the day in the tent while awake. Like with natural altitude training, there is no optimal protocol for the individual athlete, as everyone will respond slightly differently. SpO2 measures help us set individual protocols for athletes who use the tent. In [Part 3 of The Highs and Lows of Altitude Training](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/p/altitude-adaptation-health-and-ability), we discussed [the altitude classification](https://feelthebyrn.substack.com/i/131227327/altitude-classification) and how increasing elevations affect us physiologically and mentally. A SpO2 of below 70% is considered life-threatening in the medical world. In mountaineering, SpO2 values measured have been lower than that. Still, it is generally agreed that measures below 76% are unhealthy and should be avoided, particularly when exposed for prolonged periods, including sleeping overnight in an altitude tent. Good adaptations occur when SpO2 is around 86-94 for most of the night. Usually, an elevation of 2000-2400 meters will achieve this. Over time, higher altitudes can be used, subject to SpO2 readings and tolerance (sleep quality). Experienced altitude tent users, not uncommonly, get up to 4000 meters or even higher. The problem with higher altitudes is more noise from the hypoxicator and a build-up of carbon dioxide in the tent, which can cause side effects, of which fatigue and headaches are the most common. To prevent an unhealthy build-up of CO2, a CO2 scrubber can be used in the tent to remove any excess. A common starting protocol is three weeks on and one week off as follows:

Example altitude tent protocol for a first timer.

The key to using an altitude tent is **your sleep quality, not the altitude achieved (and subsequent SpO2)**. If you don’t sleep well, you will be unable to train and recover properly, and the adaptations to altitude will be in vain. The environment within an altitude tent tends to be not only hypoxic but also warm and stuffy, and the noise the hypoxicator makes can keep you awake. However, when done according to the guidelines and if tolerated, this method is considered effective, judging by the results presented by research so far.  If you are a light sleeper, this might not be for you. If you have a partner or spouse, discuss using the altitude tent beforehand, as it might impact your relationship….

args.summary:
This article is Part 6 of the "Highs & Lows of Altitude" series by Dr. John Hellemans, covering altitude simulation methods for athletic performance. It discusses three main approaches:

**Altitude Houses:** Developed in Scandinavia in the early 1990s, these are chambers at sea level that create hypoxic environments. Two methods exist: normobaric hypoxia (replacing oxygen with nitrogen, invented by Finnish scientist Heikki Rusko) and hypobaric hypoxia (reducing air pressure). Norway and Italy banned altitude simulation in 2003 over concerns about unfair advantage and safety, though Norway lifted the ban in 2021. Hypobaric chambers more closely mimic natural altitude but are less common and more expensive.

**Breath-Holding (Apnoea Training):** Voluntary breath-holding during training, primarily used by swimmers and free divers. It creates temporary hypoxia that can produce similar but lesser adaptations to altitude training, while also improving lung capacity and respiratory muscle strength. Must be practiced with caution due to blackout risk.

**Altitude Tents:** Normobaric hypoxia devices for home use. A tent fits over a bed with a hypoxicator that removes oxygen and replaces it with nitrogen. Key recommendations: 2-3 weeks minimum exposure, 12-14 hours/day, altitude of 2000-2400 meters (maintaining SpO2 of 86-94%). Sleep quality is emphasized as more important than achieving high altitude. CO2 buildup is a concern; a CO2 scrubber is recommended. A starting protocol of three weeks on, one week off is suggested.

The article notes that altitude simulation existed in Eastern Europe and Russia before WWII, with Russian pilots using intermittent hypoxic exposure. Part 2 will cover Intermittent Hypoxic Exposure and Training.
